reviews.author: Dalcomidorossi
reviews.text:
Even at a glance, the steak rice bowl is impressive in its well-balanced composition. Large slices of steak are placed on top of rice, and a glossy sauce covers the entire dish. Side dishes and soup are provided together, making it a complete meal even as a bowl of rice. Although the plating is not excessive, it is so appetizing that it makes you want to take a photo.

The most impressive part was the texture of the steak meat. It's not overly tough and feels like it softens the moment you chew it. When you take a bite, the meat is still juicy, so it goes well with the menu item called rice bowl. It is a style that anyone can enjoy comfortably as it does not have a strong spicy flavor, and the meat thickness is just right so it is good to eat with rice.

The element that enhances the perfection of steak rice bowl is the sauce. It's sweet but not overly salty, so it goes well with both rice and meat. The sauce naturally seeps into the rice, maintaining the balance of flavor until the last spoonful. Because it does not have a spicy taste, there is less discomfort after eating. It's also suitable for people who don't usually like their rice bowl sauce to be too strong.

The rice is not too tough and has a nice texture, so it serves well as a support for the steak and sauce. The texture of the rice is more important than you think in rice bowls, but the combination of rice, meat, and sauce at Furato Restaurant Steak Rice Bowl is stable. It is designed so that it tastes best when eaten together in one spoon rather than being fried separately.

Considering the prices in Seongsu-dong, the satisfaction level is high compared to the price. The amount of meat is not excessively large, but it is not enough for one meal. You can choose from both lunch and dinner, and it is recommended as an introductory menu to those visiting Furato Restaurant for the first time. There is a strong impression that it is a Japanese rice bowl restaurant that is good to visit on a daily basis rather than on special occasions.

The steak rice bowl at Seongsu branch of Furato Restaurant, a Japanese restaurant in Seongsu-dong, is a menu that stands out for its combination of tender steak, juicy meat, sweet and well-balanced sauce, and clean rice. If you want a meal that is not spicy but satisfying, it is worth choosing. If you are looking for a rice bowl menu with a low probability of failure in Seongsu-dong, it is worth considering.

Hidden Japanese restaurant

Food ★★★★★
Facilities ★★★★
Location ★★★★

It is a hidden Japanese restaurant that is difficult to find while passing by as it is located in the basement of the SK V1 building, about a 10-minute walk from Konkuk University Station.

We ordered Gyukatsu, mini curry, steak rice bowl, and soba.

First, the Gyukatsu was coated with a thin batter, cooked only on the outside, and then grilled on the sides over a mini brazier, allowing you to feel the full juiciness of the meat. Especially salt, soy sauce, special sauce? There are a total of 3 different dipping sauces, but I personally found that I enjoyed the juiciness best by adding a little salt and a little special sauce and eating it with a little wasabi and rice.

Next, the mini curry tasted like regular Japanese curry, neutralizing the unique strong taste of curry to give it a mild taste, and the garlic flakes included in the middle whetted the appetite.

And the steak rice bowl was impressive with its generous amount of meat, and the sweet seasoning enveloped my tongue.

The last soba I ordered took about 15 minutes to come out, so I had to wait a bit, but it tasted clean and gave me the feeling of finishing off the menu I had eaten so far.

reviews.author: A house that only tastes good
reviews.text:
A restaurant specializing in tsukemen
8-minute walk from Exit 4 of Children's Grand Park Station.
Tsukemen R is 9,000 won, and chashu is 2,000 won.
​
The toppings are disappointing.
Since I visited this place in 2017, I couldn't remember the taste, so I tried again.
For a Japanese ramen, it's not bad value for money.
Tsukemen is a style of eating noodles dipped in soup and is my favorite!
It's a pity that there is no chashu as a basic topping, but it is understandable since most tsukemen usually add chashu.
The noodles have a strong texture and go well with soup.
The soup has quite a bit of umami, so it tastes good.
The meat in the soup also improves its monotonous texture and taste!
The basic toppings are eggs and menma, but is it a salty soft-boiled egg rather than the ajitamago you can taste in Japanese food?
And the added chashu had a fiery scent but was cold.
The char siu tastes better when you add fire and heat with a torch at the end, but it's a shame.
As expected from a specialty restaurant, there are large pots and a slight smell of pork.
You can also eat warisup, the flower of tsukemen, which is a delicacy of tsukemen.
However, it is a bit disappointing that cold broth is provided here.
In the cold winter, pouring hot broth into leftover soup is a treat.
​
Store & Tips & Review
The store is not large and consists of counter seating.
It's a typical Japanese ramen restaurant, so it's a good place to eat alone.
When you arrive, order and pay at the kiosk at the entrance.
Please wait outside and enter according to your number.
When I visited on a Tuesday evening at 7:30, there were 5 teams waiting so I passed.
Visit at 8pm on Wednesday evening failed due to lack of ingredients.
When visiting at 7:30 pm on Thursday evening, there were 2 teams waiting.
I was able to enter after waiting for about 10 minutes.
Is it normal or does it feel like there are fewer customers on Thursday?
It is the basic taste of tsukemen, so you can eat it without any problem.

reviews.author: Chanwook Lee
reviews.text:
It is a sushi restaurant located in the Konkuk University commercial district with a Gyeonghaenggol atmosphere. Since it is located in a university area, it is very famous for its cost-effectiveness. Among Konkuk University students, there are hardly any people who don't know about it, and the regular base is quite solid.

I visited to eat the hidden menu, Omakase, and made a reservation a week in advance. Although it was roughly expected, there were so many customers that it was overwhelming and the store was almost saturated.

After confirming my reservation, I was guided to the Dachi seat, but the seat was very narrow and uncomfortable, so I often bumped into the staff walking around. They didn't even bring me the alcohol I ordered, so there were some ridiculous incidents.

The omakase started about ten minutes after we sat down, and first came seokhwa, shrimp paste, and mochiri dofu. The size of the stone was impressive and it was creamy without being fishy.

The hot-roasted dish that came out next was well-cooked on the outside, but it was slightly cooled and didn't taste good. When grilled, the heat is so great that it's hard to make it taste bad, but the inside meat is so surprisingly soft that you can't even handle it.

Next came the sashimi, including amberjack, black sea bream, pufferfish, mackerel, and flounder, all of which were two to three thick. It had a good full texture and was moderately sticky and fresh, so I was satisfied.

Next, mackerel sushi, salmon sushi, and flounder sushi came out. Salmon and flounder were common types and had basic bread, but mackerel had little fat and a slightly fishy taste.

Next to the sushi was the poached octopus leg, which was poached well, not tough and chewy, so it was edible. Since it is not a large octopus, I cannot say that it has an excellent texture.

Next came the long-awaited tuna, including Sunazuri, Mekadoro, Judodo, and Akami. Not only was it in good thawing condition overall, but it was not only thick but greasy and overflowing.

After the tuna, we moved on to sushi again, which included clam scallop sushi topped with uni, and the uni was in better condition than I expected. Although it wasn't the highest quality uni with a strong green taste, it was sweet enough.

Next, salmon roe sushi came out, and it was steaming so we could wrap it up and eat it together. Because the portion was large, I ate one bite as is and wrapped the next bite in seaweed, and I enjoyed the popping texture of the salmon roe.

Next came the tuna, which I thought was over, including the tender snazuri and grilled fish. The sunazuri aburi was oily and soft with melted tendons, and the gama meat was almost like regular Wagyu salchi.

Following the tuna, elephant clams and a few more pieces of sashimi were served at the last minute. The space was small, but the next one came so quickly that I could only take pictures of the elephant clam.

The elephant clam was boiled once, so it had a chewy texture and a slightly sweet yet strong salty taste. For some reason, it tasted even better when I dipped it in vinegar while feeling a bit drunk.

As we neared the end of the course, the eel teppanyaki came out, and honestly, it didn't taste that good. It was obvious that they used cheap imported eel, and the rich teriyaki seasoning was too sweet to the point of repulsion.

The course ended with albab and jiri stew. Jiritang was so-so because of the bland broth, but the roe-bab was not bad as it was a nostalgic taste, and the scorched rice was a subtle delicacy, so I ate it up.

Overall, the 60,000 won omakase was reasonably priced and cost-effective, but the service and space were not up to par, so it was difficult to feel highly satisfied. It's not an omakase restaurant.

As I was waiting in front of the crosswalk after exiting the Yedi University entrance, a magnificent red Chinese character sign caught my eye in the distance.
Unlike the shiny signs around it, it said, “I am the owner of this place.”
Out of curiosity, I went into the alley and found that it was a Chinese restaurant called ‘Xiyan’ that served traditional Chinese cuisine.
As I climbed the creaking stairs, opened the door, and entered, a completely different world unfolded.
Waiters, something you wouldn't see in a typical Chinese restaurant, were taking orders from customers, and the interior was very luxurious. It's probably the most luxurious restaurant I've ever eaten at.
The floor was also wooden, so it was very unique and had a vintage feel, but it turned out that this was an old store that opened in 1997.
Looking at the customers, there were students, but I also saw many professors who seemed to be regulars, so I thought this was a local restaurant.
When I sat down, the staff gave me warm jasmine tea and a side dish of jjasai, pickled radish, and onion.
When I looked at the menu, I saw that there was XO fried rice, so I ordered it right away. It's a menu item you can't get at delivery Chinese restaurants, but the price was quite reasonable at 11,000 won. Konkuk University students can eat cheaper with the 10% discount.
After waiting for about 10 minutes, the fried rice came out.
When I took a spoonful, I was struck by the rich fiery aroma, well-fried rice, and incredible umami flavor. There is something like finely chewed meat, and this is the kick. The texture is good and it's just crazy. You have to try it to know.
If you feel thirsty after eating, you can drink egg soup. The seasoning of this egg soup is just right and it makes you feel better.
Shiyen's atmosphere, taste, and service are all high-end, but the prices are reasonable, so I think I should come here often. Shiyen, an old school Chinese restaurant in Hwayang-dong, was a very successful solo eating challenge.
